explanation: A demand for something that is wanted for what it produces, not for itself. Health care is wanted because it helps produce health.
How strongly the quantity demanded reacts to a change in price: the % change in quantity divided by the % change in price.
When being insured changes behaviour: people use more care, or take less care of their health, because insurance lowers the price they face.
Making the insured person pay part of the cost of care, for example through deductibles, copayments or coinsurance.
When people know more about their own health risk than the insurer, high-risk people are more likely to buy insurance. This can push premiums up and drive low-risk people out.
The application of economic reasoning to choices, incentives and the allocation of scarce resources related to health and healthcare.
Resources spent on healthcare. It can be compared across countries as a level, per person, or as a share of GDP.
The value of the best alternative that must be given up when a choice is made.
Studying the effect of one additional unit of an activity, input or resource rather than focusing only on totals or averages.
A situation in which one party has better or more relevant information than another, such as a physician knowing more about diagnosis and treatment than a patient.
Uncertainty about future health, when care will be needed, which treatment will be appropriate, what it will cost and what outcome will follow.
A cost or benefit created by an action that affects people other than the person making the decision.
Using available resources so that avoidable waste is reduced and the greatest feasible value can be produced.
Fairness in how resources, opportunities, access or outcomes are distributed across people or groups.
Financing healthcare through a third party such as an insurer or government instead of relying only on direct payment at the point of use.
A payment made directly by a patient for healthcare rather than being fully financed by an insurer or government.
A framework linking the three central actors in healthcare: patient, provider and insurer/government.
A relationship showing how much of a good or service consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, holding other determinants constant.
The maximum amount a buyer is willing to pay for a good or service, used as a measure of how much the buyer values it.
The buyer's willingness to pay minus the amount actually paid.
A midpoint-based elasticity measure between two price-quantity points, useful for comparing responsiveness without depending on the units used.
A study that randomly assigns participants to different conditions so the groups are comparable on average before treatment.
The monetary price of care plus other costs borne by the patient, including travel costs and the opportunity cost of time.
An insurance payment that contributes a fixed amount for a covered service, leaving the patient responsible for the remaining price.
The fraction of the healthcare bill paid by the patient, with the insurer paying the rest.
A fixed amount paid by the patient each time a covered healthcare service is used.
An amount the patient pays toward medical bills before insurance reimbursement begins.
A stock representing an individual's level of health or functioning that persists over time and produces a flow of healthy or productive time.
Everything other than health that contributes to utility in the Grossman framework and is produced using time and market goods.
The low-health part of the Grossman production possibility frontier where better health releases enough sick time that health and home production can increase together.
The chosen addition to health capital during a period, denoted I in the health-stock equation.
The deterioration of inherited health capital during a period, represented by the depreciation rate δ.
Gross health investment minus depreciation. It can be negative even though gross investment itself cannot be negative.
The return to an additional unit of health capital; in the lecture the MEC is high at low health and declines as health improves.
Healthy time available for work, home production and health-producing activities after time lost to illness.
A Grossman-model case where health is valued only for the productive time it generates, not for direct utility from being healthy.

term: Demand for health vs demand for healthcare
explanation: Health is the desired stock or outcome; healthcare is one input used to produce it. Comparative statics can therefore affect the two demands differently.
A difference in health — including incidence, prevalence, mortality or burden of disease — between specific populations.
A systematic relationship in which health differs across socioeconomic position such as education, income or occupational rank.
The idea that education can improve the efficiency with which people turn time, information and healthcare inputs into health.
The idea that nutritional deprivation in utero or early life can create lasting biological adaptations that increase later disease risk when the environment changes.
A naturally occurring event or policy shock that creates comparison groups and can help study causal effects when deliberate randomization is impossible or unethical.
The hypothesis that higher income improves health by expanding the resources available for health production.
Cumulative physiological wear from prolonged or repeated stress; Session 4 links it to a higher depreciation rate of health capital.
The hypothesis that community health worsens as income becomes more unequally distributed, potentially through stress, social cohesion or political mechanisms.
A reverse-causality theory in which poor health reduces productive time, earnings and labour-force participation, thereby lowering socioeconomic status.
A third-factor explanation in which time preference influences both investment in education and investment in health.
How strongly a person values present benefits relative to future benefits; greater willingness to delay gratification can encourage long-term investment.
The principal–agent relationship in which the patient relies on a better-informed physician for advice and care.
Physician influence on patient demand for care that conflicts with the physician's own interpretation of the patient's best interest.
The tendency for a fall in physician income to make additional inducement more attractive as a way to restore income.
The tendency for a lower profit rate to make inducement less financially attractive, pushing the physician away from inducement.
A payment method that pays the provider for each service delivered.
A payment method that pays a fixed amount per enrolled patient over a period rather than paying separately for every service.
A physician payment method based primarily on fixed remuneration rather than service volume.
A physician payment arrangement combining features of more than one payment method, such as capitation with fee-for-service carve-outs.
Geographic variation in healthcare treatment or procedure rates across relatively small areas that is not fully explained by measured population needs.
A pattern of diagnostic and treatment choices shaped by physician beliefs, uncertainty and uneven diffusion of medical information.
A region of medical decision-making where evidence and guidance leave room for discretion and patient-specific judgement.
The entity on which a variable is recorded, such as a patient, admission or country. Specify it before describing or comparing the data.
Nominal categories label, ordinal categories order, interval values measure differences and ratio values also have a meaningful zero. The scale determines meaningful summaries.
The average squared deviation of the observed values from their mean, dividing by n. It describes the entered data.
The sum of squared deviations from the sample mean divided by n−1. Under independent sampling it is unbiased for population variance.
A rule assigning a percentile to ordered observations. The course np rule and Excel interpolation can produce different quartiles for the same values.
A systematic error due to who can enter or responds to a sample. Increasing sample size reduces random uncertainty but does not automatically repair bias.
F(x)=P(X≤x), the probability accumulated up to x. For a continuous model it is an area under the density, not the density height.
A variable taking 1 with probability π and 0 with probability 1−π. Its mean is π and its variance is π(1−π).
For a measurement from a normal model, z=(x−μ)/σ. For a sample mean, the denominator is its SE instead.
For independent normal measurements with unknown population variance, (X̄−μ)/(S/√n) follows t with n−1 degrees of freedom.
An estimator is a random rule before sampling, such as X̄; an estimate is its realised numerical value after sampling, such as x̄=24.2.
The distribution of an estimator across repeated samples drawn by the same design, distinct from the distribution of individual observations.
The standard deviation of an estimator’s sampling distribution. For an independent sample mean it is σ/√n, estimated with s/√n.
Under suitable conditions, standardised sample means approach a normal distribution as n grows. It does not make individual observations normal; n≥30 is only a heuristic.
The long-run proportion of intervals from a procedure that cover the fixed population parameter, under its assumptions. It is not the fraction of individual values inside an interval.
The critical value multiplied by the estimate’s SE. A symmetric confidence interval has total width twice the margin of error.
The course normal interval p̂±z√[p̂(1−p̂)/n]. Check success and failure counts; unreliable cases can give endpoints outside [0,1].
A specified statement about a population parameter that defines the test’s reference distribution, such as H₀: μ=μ₀.
The probability, assuming the null and model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability that the null is true.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis. A pre-specified significance level α controls this error probability under the test model.
The probability of rejecting a false null at a specified alternative: 1−β. It depends on effect size, uncertainty, sample size and the testing rule.
Independent groups have unrelated observations. Paired data link observations, such as repeated measurements on the same patients; analyse their differences.

term: SE of an independent mean difference
explanation: For independent groups, the estimated SE is √(s₁²/n₁+s₂²/n₂). The group order determines the sign of the contrast but not this SE.
A small p-value indicates evidence against a specified null under the model. Clinical importance depends on the effect size, outcome, context and consequences.
